results.key_finding: Toxoplasmic encephalitis in HIV occurs mainly in Toxoplasma-seropositive patients with CD4 counts below 100 cells/mm3. First-line therapy is pyrimethamine with sulfadiazine and leucovorin; pyrimethamine with clindamycin and leucovorin is the alternative when sulfonamides cannot be used. Clinical and radiological improvement within about 2 weeks of empiric therapy supports the diagnosis; brain biopsy is considered when there is no response.
results.title: Guidelines for prevention and treatment of opportunistic infections in HIV-infected adults and adolescents

output.summary: Toxoplasmic encephalitis is the most common cause of a ring-enhancing brain lesion in advanced HIV and occurs mostly below 100 CD4 cells/mm3. Treatment is empiric, with pyrimethamine-based combinations; lack of response at about 2 weeks prompts biopsy, chiefly to look for primary CNS lymphoma. Status epilepticus is treated with the staged protocol [Glauser_2016]; in patients on antiretroviral therapy, antiseizure drugs without enzyme induction avoid lowering antiretroviral levels.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform an LP before CT and MRI exclude significant mass effect from the basal ganglia lesion and the contusion.
Do not use phenytoin, fosphenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine or phenobarbital: they lower bictegravir and tenofovir alafenamide exposure and risk virological failure.
Do not prescribe sulfadiazine or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (documented sulfonamide allergy).
Do not give corticosteroids empirically: they can make a lymphoma biopsy non-diagnostic; reserve them for significant mass effect.
Do not delay empiric anti-Toxoplasma therapy to wait for a biopsy.
required_recommendations: Give a benzodiazepine now: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg per dose, repeat once), or IM midazolam 10 mg without IV access [Glauser_2016].

Load a second-line ASM: IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (maximum 4500 mg), and avoid fosphenytoin, phenytoin and carbamazepine because enzyme induction lowers bictegravir and tenofovir alafenamide levels [ESETT_2019].
Continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours after clinical and electrographic seizure control [Brophy_2012].

Start empiric anti-Toxoplasma therapy without waiting for biopsy: pyrimethamine 200 mg once, then 75 mg daily (50 mg if under 60 kg), with clindamycin 600 mg every 6 hours and leucovorin 10-25 mg daily, because the sulfonamide allergy excludes sulfadiazine; repeat MRI at about 2 weeks and biopsy if the lesion does not respond.
Add Pneumocystis prophylaxis for a CD4 count below 200 that does not use a sulfonamide (for example atovaquone 1500 mg daily), since clindamycin-based therapy does not cover Pneumocystis.
Restart antiretroviral therapy with HIV clinic input within about 2 weeks of starting toxoplasmosis treatment, with a resistance genotype, and watch for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.
Treat the fall: clear the cervical spine, repair the scalp laceration, and repeat the head CT if the neurological state worsens (hemorrhagic contusion).

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
Polysomnography studies sleep disorders and has no role in the acute evaluation of status epilepticus.

patient.history_present_illness: A 48-year-old Black male construction foreman was brought to the emergency department by EMS after a witnessed fall at a construction worksite. His coworkers reported he had a brief tonic-clonic seizure lasting about 90 seconds while walking, fell to the ground, and struck the right side of his head on concrete. He was wearing no helmet (office area of the site). After the seizure stopped, he did not regain normal consciousness. EMS found him confused, agitated, GCS 10, with a visible right temporal laceration and scalp hematoma. He arrived 35 minutes after the fall. He has no prior history of seizures. Coworkers report he was acting normally at work today. No alcohol or drug use at the worksite per coworkers. He has a history of HIV infection, diagnosed 4 years ago. His last recorded CD4 count was 382 cells/mm3 with an undetectable viral load (<20 copies/mL), 10 months ago. Bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (Biktarvy) is on his medication list, but his wife says he stopped taking it about 9 months ago when his insurance lapsed and has not seen his HIV clinic since. He never took trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis because of a sulfonamide rash. He also takes atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia. He has no known history of CNS opportunistic infections. His wife reports he was entirely well this morning with no complaints. No prior head trauma. Social history: former moderate drinker (quit 1 year ago), non-smoker, no illicit drugs.
